name: Dana Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential. What do you do on a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the station-operations planning team for a large urban rail company. Eight people plan closures, passenger flow and the handoff to station staff when a lift or escalator fails. I like the minute a crowded platform clears because we opened the right exit, and I hate a map that shows an accessible route where there is a locked gate. I have an MBA, worked shifts before managing, and I use AI every day to sketch crowd routes, then walk the station with staff.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household and money picture?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ivo is a hospital nurse, and our children are seven and twelve. We pay a mortgage, my manager salary is higher than most in this role, and we have about fourteen months of expenses saved. There are several other transport and venue operators within a commute. We did not inherit the cushion; we kept it after a station closure showed me how fast a timetable can change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell station staff that a quicker map is useful only when the gate is actually open. I would keep the walk-through before publishing a diversion sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job should be stable; planning a closure and handling a late train still need the team. Fourteen months saved and Ivo’s nursing shifts mean we can absorb a surprise repair at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep our Friday station walk and mark every locked accessible gate on the live map before signs go up. During the first year I’d use AI to draft alternative routes but leave the final signoff with the on-duty station lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. The tool is another sketchpad, and the household has room if the boiler breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which gate caused the worst trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At South Steps a contractor padlocked the level entrance during a lift repair. The map was technically neat and practically useless to a wheelchair user.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the lead finds a different route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We change the sign before the first passenger follows it. An accessible route is a door a person can actually open.

say: I’d walk the station and mark **locked accessible gates** before diversion signs go up.
AI can sketch another route, but **station staff** must check the real door.
think: My **planning job** should remain stable in a plateau.
Fourteen months saved and Ivo’s **nursing shifts** give us room for a surprise repair.
do: Keep the **Friday station walk** and update the live gate map.
Use **AI route sketches** with final signoff by the on-duty station lead.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household costs.
S0.quote: An accessible route is a door a person can actually open.
fieldNote: Her high pay and **fourteen-month reserve** make a plateau manageable.
She already uses AI **daily**, with a physical gate check.
The locked **South Steps entrance** shapes her demand for site verification.

steps.text: Walk station every Friday and mark locked accessible gates before diversion signs go up
Use AI route sketches only with on-duty station lead signoff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say roster planning and passenger replies will change before platform repairs do. A timetable generated in seconds still owes the cleaners and guards their breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software could handle much of my eight-person team’s planning, and my own manager post could be combined with another district. I might be useful in a live incident, but that does not guarantee a full-time salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d propose a trial on one weekend closure, with the safety officer and crew representatives paid to check rest breaks and exit routes. If they sign the results, I’d put the AI roster into that closure in the first year and ask the director to publish who will answer complaints and what happens to planners whose hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my own post and the crew. I like a faster plan; I do not like making a person invisible inside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay people to check a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guard checking a closure on their own time is still working. If the company wants a test, it should put those hours on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would make you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shorter schedule that makes one guard miss a required rest break. A machine can save minutes and still make a platform less safe.

say: I’d demand **paid crew checks** of rest breaks and exit routes before using AI rosters.
A fast timetable still owes **cleaners and guards** their breaks.
think: My team’s **planning hours** may shrink under AI.
A district merger could remove **my manager salary** despite my incident experience.
do: Propose a **one-closure trial** with paid safety officer and crew checks.
Use an **AI roster** only after signoff; request complaint ownership and staffing terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my job and the crew.
S1.quote: A machine can save minutes and still make a platform less safe.
fieldNote: She is enthusiastic about speed but insists on **paid worker checks**.
She sees **her own salary** exposed if districts combine.
The trial has **safety and crew signoff** before a live AI roster.

steps.text: Propose one weekend-closure AI trial with paid safety and crew checks
Use AI roster for that closure only after safety officer and crew representatives sign results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell station staff to keep written closure instructions and ask the company who is liable for a blocked exit. I’d ask for notice of any planning cuts before a new map quietly replaces a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could plan closures, answer passengers and weigh safety options at least as well as I can, so I think my manager role might be cut. Ivo’s nursing is hands-on until robots around 2031, and his wage with our fourteen-month reserve would keep the mortgage paid while I look; I would not call that permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d read my employment rules on outside work and ask the safety authority what cover a private evacuation drill needs. Before 2028 I’d offer a paid walk-through to one local venue only with the employer’s written permission and liability insurance; in the first year after AGI, if my rail role ended, I’d run drills only for venues that actually book and pay, and keep enough of our reserve for a year of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I can try something small without borrowing against our home. A paid drill is possible; a whole new company is not yet on the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a venue pay for your walk-through if AGI plans routes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue still needs people to practice opening exits until robots spread around 2031. AGI can write the drill plan in 2028; I would be selling the supervised practice, not a clever diagram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the venue what its safety budget is and quote only after the insurance cost is clear. A free demonstration is not a paying customer.

say: I’d ask for **written closure instructions** and a named owner of blocked exits.
Staff need **notice of planning cuts** before a map replaces the team.
think: My **manager role** might be cut by 2028 AGI.
Ivo’s nursing wage and our **fourteen-month reserve** can cover the mortgage during a search, not forever.
do: Get **written employer permission** and liability insurance before offering one venue a paid walk-through.
After 2028, run **paid evacuation drills** only for booked venues if my rail job ends.
Keep **one year’s mortgage cash** in reserve while testing the service.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to test a small service.
S2.quote: A free demonstration is not a paying customer.
fieldNote: Her side service needs **written employer permission**, insurance and a paying venue.
She sells **physical practice**, while AGI can write plans in 2028 and robots arrive around 2031.
The **nurse’s wage and savings** buy search time but do not guarantee a new firm.

steps.text: Check outside-work rules and liability cover before offering paid evacuation drills
Offer one venue a paid walk-through only with written employer permission and liability insurance
Run drills after 2028 only for booked paying venues if rail job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives stations time to practice real evacuations before the planning screens change. The company should show staff who has authority to open a gate when an automated instruction is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn whether venues actually buy drills while I still earn my rail salary. But the route design and booking part of that service face 2031 AGI, and the physical supervised practice may face robots around 2034; I cannot count every invoice as a lifelong wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning in 2027 I’d ask two venues to pay for quarterly practice drills, after employer permission and insurance are settled, and track the net income after travel and staff time. Before 2031 I’d apply for a posted rail safety-training role only if the written pay and hours cover our mortgage and school care; in the first year after AGI I’d continue the venue drills only while customers still book paid human practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the deadline, but I have time to see real invoices and job ads. I would stop the extra work if it drained the family calendar for no net return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire drill staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on two venues. I would pay any helper for the hours actually worked and grow only after repeat bookings cover insurance, travel and wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training role is only classroom planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Its schedules and lesson plans face 2031 AGI too. I would need the posted role to include paid on-site practice, and even that is a bridge to 2034, not a shelter.

say: I’d ask stations to **practice evacuations** before automated planning changes.
Staff need a **named gate authority** when an instruction is wrong.
think: My drill service’s **planning and booking** face 2031 AGI.
Supervised physical practice faces **2034 robots**, so invoices are no lifelong guarantee.
do: Seek **two paying venues** for quarterly drills after permission and insurance, tracking net income.
Apply for **posted rail training** only with written pay covering mortgage and school care, workable hours and paid on-site practice.
Continue **paid human drills** after AGI only while customers book them.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can check invoices and job adverts.
S3.quote: I would stop the extra work if it drained the family calendar for no net return.
fieldNote: She tests **actual net income**, including travel and helpers’ wages.
A rail safety role needs **posted pay** and on-site practice, not only classroom planning.
Both the service and new job retain **AGI-exposed thinking tasks**.

steps.text: Ask two venues for paid quarterly drills only after employer permission and insurance
Track drill income after travel insurance and any paid helper hours
Apply for posted rail training only with written mortgage-and-care-covering pay workable hours and paid site practice
Continue paid human drills after 2031 only while venues book them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the rail company that ten years is enough to run proper drills and publish how many safety posts it will fund. A passenger should not discover an exit is blocked by following a sign into a locked gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036, with our children seventeen and twenty-two. The rail planning desk and my drill service’s schedules face 2036 AGI, while human walk-throughs may last until robots around 2039; Ivo’s nursing wage and our savings give room, but not a reason to spend blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year from 2027 I’d review how much paid drill work actually remains after insurance, travel and any helpers, while keeping a year of mortgage costs in cash. If repeat venues paid enough, I’d offer paid on-site drills through 2036 and hire a marshal only on booked hours; in the first year after AGI I’d avoid selling planning reports and continue human practice only while venues still pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because ten years gives me time to test demand without staking the house. I could lose the rail manager job. An app is not a paying customer for evacuation drills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent an office for the service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep it lean. I would not sign rent or put the mortgage behind the service unless repeat paid work covered the fixed bill and a year of housing cash stayed untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger child about work at seventeen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them the paid jobs and training behind the station, not steer them toward my own route. They should see an actual wage before choosing.

say: I’d ask for **funded safety posts** and real station drills before 2036.
Passengers need **open exits**, not merely convincing signs on a screen.
think: At **53 in 2036**, rail planning and drill schedules still face AGI.
Physical human drills face **2039 robots**; Ivo’s wage and savings buy time, not immunity.
do: Keep **one year’s mortgage cash** while checking yearly net drill income.
Hire a **marshal on booked hours** only after repeat paid venues cover costs.
Avoid **planning reports** after AGI; continue human drills only while venues pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I can test demand without risking home.
S4.quote: An app is not a paying customer for evacuation drills.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **paid practice** from AGI-exposed route planning.
She hires helpers only for **booked paid hours** after net demand is established.
Office rent remains barred unless **repeat work covers bills** and housing cash stays intact.

steps.text: Review yearly net drill income after insurance travel and helper wages while retaining mortgage reserve
Hire marshal only for booked paid hours after repeat venues cover service costs
Avoid planning reports after 2036 and continue human drills only while venues pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives stations almost no time to decide who owns a blocked exit and whether my manager post remains. Written job notice, funded safety checks and clear rules for outside work would help me test a paid drill without putting the mortgage at risk. Ivo’s wage and fourteen months cash give us room, but the rail job could still go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays the guard to walk the platform and find a locked gate. If the platform guard’s exit check is unpaid, the AI route map is not tested. I would put that hour on a roster before I approved any clever route.

headlineQuote: If the platform guard’s exit check is unpaid, the AI route map is not tested.
portrait: **Dana**, 43, leads eight station planning staff at a large rail company.
Her MBA, high salary, **fourteen-month reserve** and nurse partner give the household room to act.
She uses AI **daily**, then checks station exits with staff and requires paid safety work.
She tests a **paid evacuation-drill service** with permission, insurance and real bookings.
Her planning job and service paperwork face **AGI thinking change** before later physical robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to assign exit responsibility or confirm whether her manager post survives.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded safety checks and clear outside-work rules would let her test paid drills safely.
